The display above shows how the multiplication of the matrices associated with two transformations echoes the composition of those transformations.

It is important to take care with the order in which the matrices

are written! In the representation of the composite, , the symbol for transformation T1 is on the right. To ensure that the multiplication of the associated matrices will properly echo the composition, the matrix for T1 must be on the right.

When operations in one mathematical system echo exactly operations in another, the systems are said to have the same form. The echo of composition of transformations by multiplication in the system of matrices is an example important in this and subsequent courses. The prefix “iso” means “same” and the root “morphism” means “form” or “structure.” Therefore, the echoing of composition of transformations by matrix multiplication is called

“The Matrix-Transformation Isomorphism Theorem.”

I.

Size Transformations

Transformations that produce images that are the same shape as the pre-image, though not necessarily the same size, have many important applications. In question II of assignment #21 you were introduced to a basic type of such transformations. Here is a line segment and two different images of it that meet some simple conditions:

Drawing recovered as vectorsReview candidate — compare the content and labels with the original. Reference page 6.OriginalEditable representationSVG · Drawing JSON · Original drawing

For both images of segment AB:

#1: P, A, and A' are collinear; so are P, B, and B'.

#2: The distance from P to A' is 1.5 times the distance from P to A. Also, the distance from P to B' is 1.5 times the distance from P to B.

#3: Points collinear with A and B have images collinear with A' and B'.

The transformation that produces the image segment A'B' is called a size transformation. Any size transformation must meet conditions #1 and #3 above. The special point P is called the center of the size transformation. Size transformations must also meet a condition like #2, although the number 1.5 can vary. That number is the absolute value of the magnitude of the size transformation. The sign of the magnitude of a size transformation tells whether the pre-image and image are on the same side (positive magnitude) or opposite side (negative magnitude) of the center. Now practice sketching images in both possible positions relative to the center.

VI.

Transformations Associated with a Matrix Must Map (0,0) onto Itself

If a transformation is associated with a matrix, that matrix can be used as a device to compute images. But when any 22 matrix is used to compute the image of (0,0) the result must be (0,0). Therefore if a transformation maps (0,0) to any other points besides (0,0) that transformation cannot be associated with a 22 matrix. The only translation that maps (0,0) to itself has the image formula T: T(x,y) = (x + 0, y + 0). This special translation, which maps each point to itself, is called the identity transformation.

This question is about the translation that maps (0,0) onto itself.

In the illustration above two different images of triangle ABC are shown using prime notation to represent the vertices. For either of the images, the distance from the center, P, to A' is one half the distance from P to A. Similarly, the distance from P to B' of either image is half the distance from P to B and the distance from P to C' is half the distance from P to C. Also, each image point is on the same line as the center, P, and its pre-image point.

Both of the images of triangle ABC are produced by size transformations centered at P. When the pre-image triangle and the image triangle are on the same side of the center, P, the size transformation is given a positive magnitude. Since the distance from P to an image point is half the distance from P to that point’s pre-image, the magnitude of the size transformation that maps triangle ABC onto image #1 is

Image #2 is on the opposite side of the center, P, from its pre-image, triangle ABC. When the pre-image triangle and the image triangle are on the opposite sides of the center, P, the size transformation is given a negative magnitude. Since the distance from P to any point on image #2 is one-half the distance from P to that points pre-image on triangle ABC, the magnitude for the size transformation that maps triangle ABC onto image #2 is .

II.

Computing the Area of a Right Triangle

You will probably recall using the formula A= to compute the area of a triangle. “b” represents the length of a “base” of the triangle and “h” represents the length of the altitude of the triangle drawn to the base side with length “b.”

Any side of a triangle can be designated as the “base” for the purposes of computing area. An altitude to a particular the “base” is a segment perpendicular to the line containing that base. An altitude to a base has one end on the vertex of the triangle not on that base and its other end on the line containing the base.

In the right triangle shown below, the legs are segments AC and CB. If either of the legs is taken to be a base of the triangle, the other leg is the altitude to that base. This makes the computation of the area of a right triangle particularly easy. The area of a right triangle is one-half times the product of the lengths of the legs.

Notation for Origin-Centered Rotations

It is convenient to have a special notation to represent origin-centered rotations. We will use a capital “R” to designate an origin-centered rotation and we will include a subscript to give one of the magnitudes of the rotation. A Special Notation and Image Formulas for Size Transformations centered at the Origin

Just as it is convenient to have a special notation for rotations centered at the origin, it is convenient to have a special notation for size transformations centered at the origin. A capital “S” will be used to represent origin centered size transformations. A subscript will be used to give the magnitude. For example, “S2.5” represents the origin centered size transformation with magnitude 2.5

Sk must map (1,0) onto a point collinear with (0,0) and (1,0). If k > 0, then he distance to the image must be “k” times the distance from (0,0) to (1,0). These conditions mean that the image of (1,0) must be (k,0). Similarly, the image of (0,1) must be (0,k). Therefore, the matrix associated with Sk is . From the product we can get

III.

The Effect of Positive Magnitude Size Transformations on Distance

In question V of assignment #23 you were asked to give the images of (¯1,4) and (2,0) when they are mapped with transformation S with image formula S(x, y) = (3·x, 3·y). You should recognize that S is the origin centered size transformation with magnitude 3.

The distance between the pre-images is exactly 5.

The distance between the images, (¯3, 12) and (6, 0) is exactly 15.

Notice that the distance between the two image points is equal to the magnitude times the distance between the pre-image points. This is an instance of the following fact about size transformations with positive magnitudes:

The effect of positive magnitude size transformations on distance

If points P and Q are any two points mapped with a size transformation

with positive magnitude k, the distance between the images of P and Q

is k times the distance from P to Q.

VII.

The Effect of Size Transformations with Negative Magnitudes on Length

When a segment of length 2 is mapped with a size transformation with magnitude 3 the length if its image is 3.2 = 6. However, in most mathematics courses lengths are not measured with negative numbers. We will follow the common practice in this course. Therefore if that same segment is mapped with a size transformation with magnitude ¯3, the length of the image will not be represented as ¯3.2 = ¯6.

Here is an example in a coordinate system:

Drawing recovered as vectorsThe printed A-prime and B-prime coordinate labels appear swapped relative to their drawn positions. Source labels are preserved. Reference page 23.OriginalEditable representationSVG · Drawing JSON · Original drawing

The segment has been mapped with the size transformation with magnitude ¯3 centered at the origin. That size transformation has image formula . As you can see from the computations based on the Pythagorean Theorem, the image segment, A'B' is three times the length of the pre-image segment. 3 is the absolute value of the magnitude, ¯3. Therefore the length of the image is the absolute value of the magnitude times the length of the pre-image.

The effect on length in the example above would occur with any negative magnitude. Furthermore, since the absolute value of a positive number is itself, the following is true of any size transformation, regardless of the magnitude.

When a pre-image figure with a length is mapped with a size transformation, the length of the image is the absolute value of the magnitude times the length of the pre-image.

B. What is the area of the pre-image?

C. What is the area of the image?

An Agreement About How to “Scan” a Line to Determine Whether it Rises or Falls

Drawing recovered as vectorsReview candidate — compare the content and labels with the original. Reference page 28.OriginalEditable representationSVG · Drawing JSON · Original drawing

Above is a copy of the line from question V of assignment #25. If asked whether the line appears to be “rising” or “falling,” it perhaps seems more natural to “scan” the line from left to right and describe it as “falling.” However, if the line is “scanned” from right to left, it would be described as “rising.”

In this and later mathematics courses, lines are will be used to help describe how things change. The difference between “rising” and “falling” will often be quite significant. It is therefore important that we be consistent with each other and with other users of mathematics in describing the direction of a line.

There is an established way lines are scanned. They are scanned from left to right to determine whether they will be described as “rising” or “falling.” Line in the illustration above would therefore be described as “falling.”

“Taking the Temperature” of a Line

All lines passing through the origin, except the , will pass through the vertical line described by x = 1. In this course the x = 1 line will be called the “thermometer” for lines through the origin. We will “read” the “temperature” of a line with the “thermometer” by determining the second coordinate of the point where the line intersects the thermometer.

The following facts help explain the usefulness of reading the “temperature” of line out of the origin by getting the number that indicates their vertical position of their intersection with the “thermometer”:

#1: Lines that “rise” to the right out of the origin have positive temperatures and those that “fall” have negative temperatures.

#2: The greater the absolute value of the temperature of a line, the greater is its “steepness” relative to the

Writing an Equation that Describes a Line Through the Origin

In the figure below (1,m) is used to represent the thermometer point on a “typical” line through the origin. Also shown are three images of the thermometer point, T, under origin centered size transformations. The size transformations are represented with subscripted “S’s.” The subscripts give the magnitudes of the size transformations, which are also the first coordinates of the images of T.

Drawing recovered as vectorsReview candidate — compare the content and labels with the original. Reference page 51.OriginalEditable representationSVG · Drawing JSON · Original drawing

The important thing to notice is that the second coordinate of each image point is the first coordinate of that point times “m,” the slope of line . This is not only true for the four points highlighted with dots, but it is true for all the other points on line as well. This is because any of these other points is the image of T under a size transformation centered at the origin.

Furthermore, if any point has a second coordinate that is equal to “m” times its first coordinate, that point is the image of (1,m) under a size transformation. This means that any such point is collinear with (0,0) and (1,m) and that point must be on line .

In summary, all points with second coordinates equal to their first coordinates times “m” are unique to the line through the origin with slope “m.” But these points also are all solutions of the open sentence

.

In other words, if a point is on line , then it is a solution of this open sentence. On the other hand, if a point is a solution of this open sentence it must be on line . For these two reasons, the open sentence “” is said to “describe” line .

If a line through the origin has slope “m,” the open sentence

describes that line.

I.

The Challenge of Writing Equations for Lines That do not Pass Through the Origin

One of the most commonly used mathematical skills is that of writing an equation whose solutions are all the points on a line. The result is commonly referred to as an equation for the line. In the illustration below line is parallel to line .

Drawing recovered as vectorsReview candidate — compare the content and labels with the original. Reference page 56.OriginalEditable representationSVG · Drawing JSON · Original drawing

The slope of line is the second coordinate of the image of (5,1) under the origin centered size transformation that maps that point onto the thermometer line. The magnitude of that size transformation is , the second coordinate of the image is and therefore the slope of line is . Since line passes thorough the origin, it can be described by the equation whose solutions are all those points whose second coordinates are times their first coordinates.

In general, it is rather easy to write an equation for a line that passes through the origin as long as the coordinates of at least one other point on the line is known. But line m in the illustration does not pass through the origin. However, since line m is parallel to line , its slope is , the same as the slope of line . However, is not an equation for line m since neither (¯5,3) nor (5,5) from line m are solutions of .

The bold arrows in the illustration represent two of the unlimited number of translations that will map line onto line m. Since the arrows begin at the origin, the translations they represent are easy to describe. Their image formulas are:

T1

and

T2

When either of these translations are used in this context, line is the pre-image, and is called a pre-image equation. The work you have been doing with related solutions will lead to a discovery of how to create an image equation that will have as its solutions all the points that are translated from line to line m. You will learn to create this image equation by modifying the pre-image equation in coordination with an image formula for the translation you choose to translate line onto line m.

(y + -3) = . (x + 2).

It is useful and important to see a connection between the equation that describes line , an image formula for the translation that maps line onto line , and the equation that describes line . The connection diagram shows the equations describing pre-image and image lines on the left and an image formula for mapping the pre-image to the image on the right. As this course progresses, you should develop a deeper and deeper understanding of such connection diagrams.
